title: Rise Up and Build
subtitle: Ezra & Nehemiah in Poems & Pictures
author: Timothy Holt
beforeYouBegin:
Ezra and Nehemiah begin with a king's decree and a long road home, and end with a finished wall and a people hearing their story read aloud again. In between: gold bowls counted out one by one, a foundation laid to shouting and weeping, a scribe bent over a scroll, a cup bearer who could not hide his sadness, a night ride along broken walls, builders with a tool in one hand, and a whole city sleeping under branches on its rooftops.

This book walks through it in forty short poems, in five parts, two for Ezra and three for Nehemiah. Each poem sits beside a picture and under a single line of Scripture. The pictures stay with the things the story touches—an altar of uncut stones, a balance scale, a wine cup, a trowel beside a wall—and leave the faces to your imagination.

The poems are not the Bible. They are one reader's response to it. Open the books of Ezra and Nehemiah alongside this book, and let the real words have the last word.

parts.title: For He Is Good
parts.epigraph: For he is good, for his loving kindness endures forever toward Israel.
parts.lightName: Light of For He Is Good
parts.lightHint: Near 'stirred' (Ezra 1:1–2) in Part 1: For He Is Good

parts.title: The Good Hand of Our God
parts.epigraph: The hand of our God was on us, and he delivered us from the hand of the enemy and the bandit by the way.
parts.lightName: Light of The Good Hand of Our God
parts.lightHint: Near 'set his heart' (Ezra 7:10) in Part 2: The Good Hand of Our God

parts.title: A Sad Face Before the King
parts.epigraph: So I prayed to the God of heaven.
parts.lightName: Light of A Sad Face Before the King
parts.lightHint: Near 'the wall is broken' (Nehemiah 1:2–4) in Part 3: A Sad Face Before the King

parts.title: A Mind to Work
parts.epigraph: So we built the wall; and all the wall was joined together to half its height: for the people had a mind to work.
parts.lightName: Light of A Mind to Work
parts.lightHint: Near 'across from his own house' (Nehemiah 3:28–32) in Part 4: A Mind to Work

parts.title: The Joy of Yahweh
parts.epigraph: Go your way. Eat the fat, drink the sweet, and send portions to him for whom nothing is prepared, for today is holy to our Lord.
parts.lightName: Light of The Joy of Yahweh
parts.lightHint: Near 'all the people stood' (Nehemiah 8:1–6) in Part 5: The Joy of Yahweh

paintings.title: stirred
paintings.epigraph: “Yahweh stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia”
paintings.poem:
a long time
to live in someone else's city,
to hang your harps
on someone else's trees.

then one morning
the most powerful man in the world
put his name to a strange idea:

let them go home.
let them build.

he may have thought
it was his idea.

it was a promise
God had made through Jeremiah
long before.

the heart of a king
is a small thing
for God to stir.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Sometimes a single sentence opens a window in a closed room: how does “the heart of a king is a small thing for God to stir” (Ezra 1:1–2) speak to a question you have been carrying lately?

paintings.title: strengthened their hands
paintings.epigraph: “All those who were around them strengthened their hands”
paintings.poem:
not everyone went.

perhaps some were too old
for the road.
some had built houses there,
and planted gardens.

but the ones who stayed
did more than wave.

they pressed silver
into the travelers' hands,
and gold, and goods,
and animals for the long walk.

some of us are sent.
some of us send.

both are
how the house gets built.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Hold your hands open for a moment before “strengthened their hands” (Ezra 1:5–6): what are you gripping tightly that loosens when you hear, “both are how the house gets built”?

paintings.title: counted out
paintings.epigraph: “counted them out to Sheshbazzar, the prince of Judah.”
paintings.poem:
bowls of gold.
platters of silver.

carried off to Babylon
and set in the house
of another god,

where they sat for years,
far from the altar
they were made for.

then someone came with a list
and counted them out,
one by one—
five thousand four hundred—
and sent them home.

nothing that belongs to God
is ever lost
to him.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Scripture remembers this moment in Ezra 1:7–11 not to impress us, but to steady us: when have you seen the truth that “nothing that belongs to God is ever lost to him” in your own story?

paintings.title: on its base
paintings.epigraph: “they set the altar on its base”
paintings.poem:
no temple yet.
no walls.
just rubble and weeds
and neighbors watching.

they were afraid.
the text says so.

they built the altar anyway,
right where it belonged,
and lit the morning fire,
and the evening one.

before the roof,
before the doors,
before anything was safe—

worship.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As your pilgrim lantern pauses at “on its base” (Ezra 3:2–3), what one honest sentence would you pray beside the warmth of the fire after reading, “before the roof, before the doors, before anything was safe— worship”?

paintings.title: cedar
paintings.epigraph: “to bring cedar trees from Lebanon to the sea, to Joppa”
paintings.poem:
silver for the masons.
oil for Sidon and Tyre.

and the cedars came down
from the mountains
and out to sea,
floated along the coast
to Joppa,

the way they came
for Solomon.

new work.
old road.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Between the opening line (“silver for the masons”) and the closing thought (“and the cedars came down from the mountains and out to sea, floated along the coast to Joppa, the way they came for Solomon. new work. old road”), what is Ezra 3:7 gently reframing in your own day?

paintings.title: a great shout
paintings.epigraph: “All the people shouted with a great shout”
paintings.poem:
one course of stone.
that's all it was.

a line of blocks
in the dirt
where a house would be.

but the priests lifted trumpets,
and the Levites struck cymbals,
and they sang it back and forth
across the site:

he is good.
his loving kindness
endures forever.

and the people shouted
as if the whole thing
were already finished.

sometimes faith
is just a lot of noise
over a foundation.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Along the road of Rise Up and Build, “a great shout” (Ezra 3:10–11) slows us down at the clear note of the horn to remind us: “sometimes faith is just a lot of noise over a foundation.” Where are you being invited to trade control for trust today?

paintings.title: the old men wept
paintings.epigraph: “the people could not discern the noise of the shout of joy from the noise of the weeping of the people”
paintings.poem:
the young ones shouted.

but the old men
had seen the first house.
they looked at this
small beginning
and wept out loud.

and from far away
no one could tell
which was which—
the joy, the grief,
one sound
rising off the hill.

most beginnings
sound like that.
let both be heard.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: If you were walking this road with a close friend and stopped at “the old men wept” (Ezra 3:12–13), what would you talk about after reading, “most beginnings sound like that. let both be heard”?

paintings.title: work stopped
paintings.epigraph: “Then the people of the land weakened the hands of the people of Judah, and troubled them in building.”
paintings.poem:
counselors were hired.
letters were written.
hands grew weak.

and the work stopped.

not for a week.
for years.

grass grew up
between the stones
they had shouted over.

if your work
has stopped,
if the thing you began with joy
sits in the weeds—

it is not finished.
it is waiting.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Pause before your own two hands: what changes in your posture today when you sit with the closing words of “work stopped”—“if your work has stopped, if the thing you began with joy sits in the weeds— it is not finished. it is waiting”?

paintings.title: helping them
paintings.epigraph: “with them were the prophets of God, helping them.”
paintings.poem:
the prophets did not stand
at a distance
and point.

Haggai and Zechariah
spoke in God's name,

and Zerubbabel and Jeshua
rose up
and started again,

and the prophets
were right there with them,
helping.

a word from God
often shows up
with dust on it.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Look at the stillness of the dust of the road in Timothy’s painting: what striving can you lay down as you ponder, “a word from God often shows up with dust on it” (Ezra 5:1–2)?

paintings.title: the eye of their God
paintings.epigraph: “But the eye of their God was on the elders of the Jews”
paintings.poem:
the governor rode up
with questions.

who told you to build this?
what are your names?

they answered plainly:
we are servants
of the God of heaven and earth.

and while the letter
traveled to the king
and back,

no one made them stop.

someone was watching them
more closely
than the governor.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In Ezra 5:3–5, the story turns on the name by which He calls you—and ends with, “someone was watching them more closely than the governor.” What small, unhurried faithfulness is God inviting you into today?

paintings.title: a scroll at Achmetha
paintings.epigraph: “A scroll was found at Achmetha”
paintings.poem:
the governor had asked
for a search,
to see if the story was true.

and somewhere in Media,
in a palace archive,
on a shelf no one had touched
in years,

a scroll was waiting.

the decree of Cyrus.
let the house be built.
let the king pay for it.

they went looking
for a problem.

they found
the promise.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: The world measures life by speed and noise, yet Ezra 6:1–3 points us to the unrolled parchment and whispers, “let the king pay for it. they found the promise.” How can you practice that unhurried wisdom today?

paintings.title: made joyful
paintings.epigraph: “Yahweh had made them joyful”
paintings.poem:
it was finished
on the third day of Adar.

a house of stone
where for years there had been
only a foundation.

they dedicated it with joy.
they kept the Passover
and the feast of unleavened bread.

and the text is careful
to say where the joy
came from:

Yahweh
had made them joyful.

they built the house.
he built the gladness.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: The poem closes with a quiet turn: “and the text is careful to say where the joy came from: Yahweh had made them joyful. he built the gladness.” Where in your life right now does that line hit closest to home?

paintings.title: set his heart
paintings.epigraph: “For Ezra had set his heart to seek Y ahweh’s law, and to do it, and to teach statutes and ordinances in Israel.”
paintings.poem:
seek.
do.
teach.
in that order.

he did not teach
what he had not tried.
he did not try
what he had not searched for.

he set his heart
the way you set a stone—
bent over the scroll
by lamplight,
far from Jerusalem,

getting ready
for a road
he did not yet know
he would walk.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Sometimes a single sentence opens a window in a closed room: how does “he set his heart the way you set a stone— bent over the scroll by lamplight, far from Jerusalem, getting ready for a road he did not yet know he would walk” (Ezra 7:10) speak to a question you have been carrying lately?

paintings.title: the good hand
paintings.epigraph: “according to the good hand of his God on him.”
paintings.poem:
the first day of the first month,
they left Babylon.

the first day of the fifth month,
they walked into Jerusalem.

four months of road.
dust and heat
and little ones asking
how much farther.

Ezra doesn't tell us
about the blisters.

he just says,
more than once,
the good hand
of his God
was on him.

for him
that was the whole story
of the trip.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Hold your hands open for a moment before “the good hand” (Ezra 7:8–9): what are you gripping tightly that loosens when you hear, “for him that was the whole story of the trip”?

paintings.title: ashamed to ask
paintings.epigraph: “So we fasted and begged our God for this: and he granted our request.”
paintings.poem:
he had told the king,
our God's hand is on
all who seek him.

so how could he turn around
and ask for soldiers?

he was ashamed to.

so they camped by the river
with their little ones
and their silver and gold
and a dangerous road ahead,

and they fasted,
and they asked.

and God answered.

sometimes faith
means living inside
what you already said
out loud.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Scripture remembers this moment in Ezra 8:21–23 not to impress us, but to steady us: when have you seen the truth that “sometimes faith means living inside what you already said out loud” in your own story?

paintings.title: holy vessels
paintings.epigraph: “You are holy to Yahweh, and the vessels are holy.”
paintings.poem:
he weighed it all out:
silver, gold,
bowls,
two vessels of bright bronze.

then he looked
at the twelve priests
who would carry it

and said,
you are holy to Yahweh.
and the vessels are holy.

watch them.
keep them.

he said it about the cups.

he said it about the men
first.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As your pilgrim lantern pauses at “holy vessels” (Ezra 8:24–30), what one honest sentence would you pray beside the quiet centerpiece of “holy vessels” after reading, “he said it about the men first”?

paintings.title: a nail in his holy place
paintings.epigraph: “Now for a little moment grace has been shown from Y ahweh our God”
paintings.poem:
he tore his robe
and sat stunned
until the evening offering.

then he knelt,
spread out his hands,
and told the truth:
our guilt has grown
up to the heavens.

and still, in the middle of it:
a little grace.
a remnant.
a nail in his holy place—

something small,
driven into the wall
so it holds.

enough to hang
a life on.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Between the opening line (“he tore his robe and sat stunned until the evening offering”) and the closing thought (“a remnant. enough to hang a life on”), what is Ezra 9:5–9 gently reframing in your own day?

paintings.title: in the great rain
paintings.epigraph: “trembling because of this matter, and because of the great rain.”
paintings.poem:
the ninth month.
cold rain.
everyone sitting in the open square
before God's house,
shivering.

they had a hard thing to face.
this is not the work
of one day or two,
they said.

the book of Ezra
ends with a list of names
and a line about their children.
it doesn't tell us
how every family fared.

some pages
are for grieving,
and for trusting God
with what we can't see.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Along the road of Rise Up and Build, “in the great rain” (Ezra 10:9–13) slows us down at the name by which He calls you to remind us: “some pages are for grieving, and for trusting God with what we can't see.” Where are you being invited to trade control for trust today?

paintings.title: the wall is broken
paintings.epigraph: “When I heard these words, I sat down and wept”
paintings.poem:
he had a good post
in the palace at Susa.

his brother came from Judah,
and he asked,
how is the city?

the wall is broken down.
the gates are burned.

he could have said, that's too bad,
and gone back to work.
instead he sat down
and wept, for days.

a calling
often starts
as an ache
you can't put down.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: If you were walking this road with a close friend and stopped at “the wall is broken” (Nehemiah 1:2–4), what would you talk about after reading, “a calling often starts as an ache you can't put down”?

paintings.title: day and night
paintings.epigraph: “Let your ear now be attentive, and your eyes open”
paintings.poem:
he prayed day and night.
he said we.
I and my father's house have sinned.

he reminded God
of God's own words:
if you return,
I will gather you,
even from the farthest edge
of the heavens.

then one small, specific request:
grant me mercy
in the sight of this man.

and the last line of the chapter:
I was cup bearer to the king.

he knew which door
he was praying toward.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Pause before the open threshold: what changes in your posture today when you sit with the closing words of “day and night”—“he knew which door he was praying toward”?

paintings.title: a sad face
paintings.epigraph: “Why is your face sad, since you are not sick?”
paintings.poem:
months had passed.
he poured the wine
the way he always did,
but this time
he couldn't hide it.

he had never been sad
before the king.
in that court, perhaps,
a sad face was a dangerous thing.

why is your face sad?
and Nehemiah
was very much afraid.

you can be afraid
and still tell the truth.
that is often
where the door opens.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Look at the stillness of the open threshold in Timothy’s painting: what striving can you lay down as you ponder, “that is often where the door opens” (Nehemiah 2:1–2)?

paintings.title: between the question and the answer
paintings.epigraph: “Then the king said to me, “What is your request?””
paintings.poem:
the king asked,
what do you want?

and between the question
and the answer
there was a breath.

so I prayed
to the God of heaven.

no kneeling.
no time.
a prayer
the size of a heartbeat,

and then he spoke.

you don't always
get to close your eyes.

God hears
the short ones too.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In Nehemiah 2:4–5, the story turns on the quiet rhythm of your breath—and ends with, “God hears the short ones too.” What small, unhurried faithfulness is God inviting you into today?

paintings.title: the night ride
paintings.epigraph: “I arose in the night, I and a few men with me.”
paintings.poem:
three days in the city.
then, in the night,
he went out,
telling no one
what God had put in his heart.

a few men,
one animal,
and the moon.

out the valley gate,
past the jackal's well,
along the broken wall,
until there was no room
for his animal to pass.
so he went up by the brook
and kept looking.

before you build,
you have to see the whole ruin
and not look away.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: The world measures life by speed and noise, yet Nehemiah 2:12–15 points us to the quiet brook and whispers, “before you build, you have to see the whole ruin and not look away.” How can you practice that unhurried wisdom today?

paintings.title: the good work
paintings.epigraph: “So they strengthened their hands for the good work.”
paintings.poem:
come, he said.
you see it too.
let's build.

and they answered,
let's rise up and build.

the mockers came right away:
will you rebel?

the God of heaven
will prosper us,
he said.
we will arise and build.

it takes one person
to see the ruin.
it takes everyone
to say let's.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: The poem closes with a quiet turn: “it takes everyone to say let's.” Where in your life right now does that line hit closest to home?

paintings.title: across from his own house
paintings.epigraph: “the priests made repairs, everyone across from his own house.”
paintings.poem:
the priests built the sheep gate.
goldsmiths built a stretch.
perfumers built a stretch.
the men of Jericho,
the men of Tekoa,
rulers of half a district.

and here and there
someone mended the wall
across from his own house.

no one rebuilt
the whole city.

each one took the piece
in front of him.

that's how a wall
goes all the way around.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Sometimes a single sentence opens a window in a closed room: how does “that's how a wall goes all the way around” (Nehemiah 3:28–32) speak to a question you have been carrying lately?

paintings.title: and his daughters
paintings.epigraph: “he and his daughters, made repairs.”
paintings.poem:
a long list
of fathers and sons,

and then,
tucked in the middle,

Shallum,
he and his daughters.

their names aren't given.

their stones
are still in the wall.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Hold your hands open for a moment before “and his daughters” (Nehemiah 3:12): what are you gripping tightly that loosens when you hear, “their stones are still in the wall”?

paintings.title: if a fox
paintings.epigraph: “if a fox climbed up it, he would break down their stone wall.”
paintings.poem:
what are these feeble Jews doing?
will they finish in a day?
will they bring stones back to life
out of burned rubble?

and his friend laughed:
a fox could knock it over.

they weren't wrong
about the stones.
burned, cracked, small.

they were wrong
about the builders,
and about the One
they were building for.

keep building.

let the fox
say what he likes.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Scripture remembers this moment in Nehemiah 4:1–3 not to impress us, but to steady us: when have you seen the truth that “let the fox say what he likes” in your own story?

paintings.title: much rubble
paintings.epigraph: “The strength of the bearers of burdens is fading, and there is much rubble”
paintings.poem:
halfway up,
the complaint came.

we're tired.
there's too much rubble.
we can't do this.

and it was true.
half a wall
is a lot of wall
still to go.

Nehemiah didn't argue
with the tiredness.

he set a watch,
and said,
don't be afraid.
remember the Lord.

and they all went back
to the wall,
each one to his work.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As your pilgrim lantern pauses at “much rubble” (Nehemiah 4:10–15), what one honest sentence would you pray beside the stones of the wall after reading, “and they all went back to the wall, each one to his work”?

paintings.title: one hand
paintings.epigraph: “everyone with one of his hands did the work, and with the other held his weapon.”
paintings.poem:
a trowel in one hand.
a weapon in the other.
a sword at every side.

building
and watching
at the same time.

you may know this life:
the job and the battle
on the same day,
in the same two hands.

nobody got
to put down the work.
nobody got
to stop keeping watch.

and the wall
still went up.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Between the opening line (“a trowel in one hand”) and the closing thought (“and the wall still went up”), what is Nehemiah 4:16–18 gently reframing in your own day?

paintings.title: the trumpet
paintings.epigraph: “Our God will fight for us.”
paintings.poem:
the wall is long,
and we are spread thin,
far from one another.

so listen for the trumpet.

wherever it sounds,
run there.

no one on the wall
was meant
to stand alone.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Along the road of Rise Up and Build, “the trumpet” (Nehemiah 4:19–20) slows us down at the stones of the wall to remind us: “no one on the wall was meant to stand alone.” Where are you being invited to trade control for trust today?

paintings.title: even today
paintings.epigraph: “Please restore to them, even today”
paintings.poem:
while the wall went up,
a cry went up too.

fields mortgaged for grain.
sons and daughters
given into bondage
to their own people.

Nehemiah was very angry.
what good is a wall
if inside it
brothers are selling brothers?

give it back, he said.
the fields, the vineyards,
the olive groves, the houses.
even today.

and they said,
we will.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: If you were walking this road with a close friend and stopped at “even today” (Nehemiah 5:1–11), what would you talk about after reading, “the fields, the vineyards, the olive groves, the houses. and they said, we will”?

paintings.title: a great work
paintings.epigraph: “I am doing a great work, so that I can’t come down.”
paintings.poem:
come down,
they said.
let's meet in the plain.
let's talk.

they meant him harm.

four times they asked.
four times
he gave the same answer:

I am doing a great work.
I can't come down.

not every invitation
is a door.

some are only
a ladder
down.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Pause before the stone pillow at Bethel: what changes in your posture today when you sit with the closing words of “a great work”—“some are only a ladder down”?

paintings.title: fifty-two days
paintings.epigraph: “So the wall was finished in the twenty-fifth day of Elul, in fifty-two days.”
paintings.poem:
fifty-two days.

tired hands,
burned stones,
mockers on every side,
a sword beside every trowel.

fifty-two days,
and not one gap
left in it.

and the neighbors
who had laughed
lost their nerve,

because they could see it
as plainly as the stones:

this work
was done
by our God.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Look at the stillness of your own two hands in Timothy’s painting: what striving can you lay down as you ponder, “and the neighbors who had laughed lost their nerve, because they could see it as plainly as the stones: this work was done by our God” (Nehemiah 6:15–16)?

paintings.title: all the people stood
paintings.epigraph: “when he opened it, all the people stood up.”
paintings.poem:
the wall was done.
then all the people
gathered as one
in the square by the water gate
and asked Ezra
to bring the book.

he climbed a platform of wood
built for the day,
and when he opened it,
everyone stood.

from early morning
until midday,
men and women
and all who could understand,
ears open
to the God
who had brought them home.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In Nehemiah 8:1–6, the story turns on the stones of the wall—and ends with, “from early morning until midday, men and women and all who could understand, ears open to the God who had brought them home.” What small, unhurried faithfulness is God inviting you into today?

paintings.title: gave the sense
paintings.epigraph: “they gave the sense, so that they understood the reading.”
paintings.poem:
the Levites moved
among the people,

reading it clearly,
explaining it,
until the words
made sense.

and when they understood,
they wept.

it is one thing
to hear the law.

it is another
to hear it
and know
it is talking about you.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: The world measures life by speed and noise, yet Nehemiah 8:7–9 points us to the quiet centerpiece of “gave the sense” and whispers, “it is another to hear it and know it is talking about you.” How can you practice that unhurried wisdom today?

paintings.title: your strength
paintings.epigraph: “Don’t be grieved, for the joy of Yahweh is your strength.”
paintings.poem:
don't weep today.
today is holy.

go home.
eat the rich food.
drink something sweet.
send a portion
to the one
who has nothing ready.

the joy of Yahweh
is your strength.

your joy in him, yes.
and maybe more:
his gladness,
holding you up
on the days
your own runs out.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: The poem closes with a quiet turn: “and maybe more: his gladness, holding you up on the days your own runs out.” Where in your life right now does that line hit closest to home?

paintings.title: booths on the roofs
paintings.epigraph: “There was very great gladness.”
paintings.poem:
the next day
they read about the booths,

so they went out to the hills
for olive branches,
myrtle, palm,

and built shelters
on their roofs,
in their courtyards,
in the open squares.

a whole city
sleeping under leaves,
remembering the wilderness.

no one had done it like this
since the days of Joshua.

there was
very great gladness.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Sometimes a single sentence opens a window in a closed room: how does “there was very great gladness” (Nehemiah 8:14–17) speak to a question you have been carrying lately?

paintings.title: their clothes did not wear out
paintings.epigraph: “They lacked nothing. Their clothes didn’t grow old, and their feet didn’t swell.”
paintings.poem:
they stood
and told the whole story,
and it was not
a flattering one.

stiff necks.
a molded calf.
turning back,
again and again.

and between every failure,
the same line:
but you didn't forsake them.

forty years in the wilderness,
and their clothes didn't wear out,
and their feet didn't swell.

a God ready to pardon.
that's the only reason
anyone was left to tell it.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Hold your hands open for a moment before “their clothes did not wear out” (Nehemiah 9:16–21): what are you gripping tightly that loosens when you hear, “that's the only reason anyone was left to tell it”?

paintings.title: heard far away
paintings.epigraph: “the joy of Jerusalem was heard even far away.”
paintings.poem:
two great choirs
went up on the wall
and walked it
in opposite directions,
giving thanks,
until both stood
in the house of God.

trumpets, harps, cymbals.
the women.
the children.

years before,
at the first foundation,
the shouting and the weeping
could not be told apart.

this time it was joy,
and it was heard
far away.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Scripture remembers this moment in Nehemiah 12:31–43 not to impress us, but to steady us: when have you seen the truth that “this time it was joy, and it was heard far away” in your own story?

paintings.title: remember me
paintings.epigraph: “Remember me, my God, for good.”
paintings.poem:
it doesn't end
with a parade.

Nehemiah went back to the king,
and when he returned,
things had slipped:
an enemy given a room
in the house of God,
the singers gone to their fields,
the Sabbath sold like any day.

so he started again.
emptied the room.
called the Levites back.
shut the gates at dusk.

and the last words of the book
aren't about the wall.
they're a man asking God,
one more time,
remember me for good.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As your pilgrim lantern pauses at “remember me” (Nehemiah 13:7–31), what one honest sentence would you pray beside the stones of the wall after reading, “they're a man asking God, one more time, remember me for good”?
